Their identities ultimately merge within the imagined landscape, suggesting that art and storytelling preserve connection and create a semblance of life despite loss and confinement.

Keywords: Sarah, The, Gillyflowers

outputs.L1:
*(For Sarah, when she’s older)*

The round, sad-eyed man puffed cigars as if he were alive. Gillyflowers stood to the left of the apple, purple bells to the right, and a grass-covered hill behind.

“I am sad today,” said the sad-eyed man, “for I have locked my head in a Japanese box and lost the key. I am sad today,” he told me, “for there are gillyflowers by the apple and purple bells I cannot see. Will you look at them for me,” he asked, “and tell me what you find?”

“I cannot,” I replied, “for my eyes have grown sugary and dim from reading too long by candlelight.”

“Then tell me what you’ve read,” said the round, sad-eyed man.

“I cannot,” I replied, “for my memory has grown tired and dim from looking at things that cannot be seen by any kind of light. And I have locked my head in a Japanese box and thrown away the key.”

“Then I am you, and you are me,” said the sad-eyed man, as if alive. “I’ll write you in where I should be—between the gillyflowers and the purple bells, the apple and the hill—and we’ll puff cigars from noon till night as if we were alive.”
outputs.L2:
*(For Sarah to read when she is older)*

A plump man with mournful eyes smoked cigars, giving the impression that he was living. Beside an apple, gillyflowers bloomed on one side and violet bells on the other, while a hill blanketed in grass rose behind them.

“Today I feel sorrowful,” the melancholy-eyed man said, “because I shut my head inside a Japanese box and misplaced the key. I am also unhappy because gillyflowers grow beside the apple, along with purple bells that I am unable to see. Would you look at them in my place and describe what you discover?”

“That is impossible,” I answered. “Too many hours spent reading by candlelight have made my eyes sweetly clouded and weak.”

“In that case,” said the round man with the sorrowful gaze, “tell me what you have been reading.”

“I cannot do that either,” I replied. “My memory has become weary and obscure from contemplating things invisible in every kind of illumination. Besides, I locked my own head inside a Japanese box and cast away its key.”

“Then you must be me, and I must be you,” the sad-eyed man declared, almost as though he truly lived. “I will place you in the picture where I belong—among the apple, the gillyflowers, the purple bells, and the hill. Together we will smoke cigars from midday until darkness, pretending that we are alive.”
outputs.L3:
A round, sad-eyed man appears in a picturesque landscape surrounded by gillyflowers, purple bells, an apple, and a hill covered in grass. Yet he cannot enjoy any of this beauty. He explains that he has locked his head inside a Japanese box, misplaced the key, and is therefore unable to see the flowers around him.

The man asks the speaker to describe the scene, but the speaker is equally limited. Their eyesight has grown dim after too much reading by candlelight, and they can no longer remember what they have read. Their memory has been exhausted by prolonged contemplation of things that lie beyond ordinary human sight.

Recognizing that both of them are cut off from the world—one unable to see and the other unable either to see clearly or remember—the man declares that they are fundamentally the same. He imagines placing the speaker beside him within the landscape, where the two of them will sit together and puff cigars “as if” they were alive. The phrase gives the imagined companionship an eerie quality, suggesting that both figures occupy a state suspended between life and unreality.

### The Painted Country

By the time I found him, I was tired enough to mistake the painting for a window.

It hung at the end of a dim corridor in a house where every room seemed to have forgotten its purpose. Dust softened the furniture. Clocks stood with their hands folded at different hours. Outside, rain dragged its fingers down the glass, though I could no longer remember when the storm had begun.

The painting showed a narrow country beneath a colorless sky. A road curved between black trees and vanished behind a low hill. Beside the road sat a man in a dark coat, his hands resting on his knees. His eyes were so full of sorrow that I looked away.

“Don’t,” he said.

I turned back. His lips had not moved, yet I had heard him clearly.

“Don’t look away,” he repeated. “It makes the dark come sooner.”

I stepped closer. The paint was cracked around the edges, and flakes of sky had fallen away, revealing bare canvas like old bone.

“Are you speaking to me?”

“Who else is there?”

I glanced down the corridor. The house answered with the settling of boards.

The man smiled faintly. “You see?”

I asked him how long he had been there.

“That depends,” he said, “on which side of the frame you mean.”

He rose stiffly. Behind him, the trees shifted although there was no wind. Each had a small brass lock fixed to its trunk. Hundreds of keys hung from the branches, chiming soundlessly.

“What are those?”

“Minds,” he said. “Or doors to minds. I’ve never been able to decide.”

“Why are they locked?”

“For safekeeping.”

“From what?”

“From one another.”

He walked toward the nearest tree and reached for a key, but his hand passed through it in a smear of gray paint. When he drew it back, two of his fingers were missing. He studied the blank place without surprise.

“I used to know which key was mine,” he said.

The corridor seemed colder. I rubbed my eyes, and for a moment the picture dissolved into a confusion of shadows. When my sight cleared, the man was nearer the frame.

“You’re fading,” I told him.

“So are you.”

I laughed, because weariness sometimes turns fear into something that sounds like laughter. “I’m standing here.”

“That is not proof.”

I wanted to leave, but the corridor behind me had grown longer. The lamps had gone out one by one, and the door through which I had entered was no more than a pale square in the distance.

The man looked at me with his sad eyes.

“Tell me something,” he said.

“What?”

“Anything you remember.”

I tried to summon a face. My mother’s, perhaps, or the face of a woman I had once loved. I found only fragments: a blue sleeve, the gleam of a spoon, sunlight on a forehead. The more fiercely I searched, the more the fragments retreated.

“There was a garden,” I said at last.

At once, a patch of yellow flowers appeared beside the painted road.

“What kind?” he asked.

“I don’t know.”

The flowers paled.

“Don’t stop.”

“There was a wall covered in ivy. A red gate. Someone waited beyond it.”

The hill in the painting opened, and a wall rose from the earth. Ivy crept across it in green threads. A red gate swung gently on its hinges.

“Who waited there?”

I pressed my hands against my temples. Something moved behind my eyes like a bird trapped in a locked room.

“I can’t see.”

“Then invent.”

So I told him there was a child behind the gate, though I did not know whether that was true. The child held a paper boat. Her hair was dark. One shoe was untied. She was waiting for someone who had promised to return before the rain.

The child appeared exactly as I described her.

The man watched with wonder.

“You made her alive,” he whispered.

“No. I only spoke.”

“Perhaps that is the same thing here.”

The rain in the corridor began to fall inside the house. It dripped from the ceiling and ran down the wallpaper, blurring the faded patterns. My vision narrowed. The edges of the frame swam in darkness.

“Now you tell me something,” I said.

He looked toward the painted horizon.

“I remember a room,” he said slowly. “A chair beside a bed. A book lying open, though no one was reading. There was an old man in the bed, and someone sat with him through the night.”

The landscape changed. On the hill, a small house appeared, one window lit.

“Who was the old man?”

“I don’t know.”

“And the one beside him?”

“I don’t know that either.”

His face tightened with pain. A crack ran through the painted sky.

“Perhaps one was you,” I said.

“Which one?”

I could not answer.

The corridor trembled. The clocks throughout the house began striking at once, each announcing a different hour. With every chime, something vanished from the painting: the child’s paper boat, the red gate, the flowers, the road behind the hill.

The man gripped the inner edge of the frame.

“Keep talking.”

“I have nothing left.”

“Make something.”

So I made a river. I gave it silver water and white stones. I placed birds above it, though I could no longer remember the shape of wings. I told of a bridge leading to a town where every window remained lit for those who had lost their way.

As I spoke, the river cut through the painted earth. The birds rose awkwardly into the sky. Far away, lights trembled into being.

The man stepped backward into this new country.

“Come with me,” he said.

“I can’t.”

“You’re already here.”

I looked down. My hands were flat and colorless. The rain passed through them. Behind me, the corridor had become a thin strip of darkness bordered by wood.

I could no longer tell whether I stood before the painting or inside it.

The man held out his hand. This time, when I took it, neither of us passed through the other.

His face seemed familiar now. The line of his mouth, the weariness around his eyes—these were details I had seen every morning, perhaps in a mirror, perhaps in a dream. Or perhaps he had borrowed them from me while I spoke.

“Are you the old man in the bed?” I asked.

“I might be.”

“Am I the one who sat beside him?”

“You might be.”

“Which of us is remembering?”

He smiled sadly. “Does it matter?”

Behind us, the frame shrank until it was no larger than a distant doorway. Through it I saw the empty corridor, the silent clocks, and a chair placed before the painting. Someone sat in the chair with his head bowed. Whether he slept or had died, I could not tell.

The sad-eyed man and I walked toward the town.

With each step, I felt him entering my thoughts, or myself entering his. His lost rooms opened inside me. My invented river flowed through him. Soon I could no longer say who had imagined the child at the gate or who had waited beside the bed. We became two voices telling the same story, then one voice speaking to keep silence away.

The painted country remained narrow. Its sky was still cracked. Beyond the town there might have been nothing but canvas and dark.

Yet the windows were lit.

The river moved.

And as long as we continued to name the trees, the road, the vanished faces, and one another, the birds kept circling overhead—poorly drawn, half remembered, but alive enough to fly.

### Sarah and the Gillyflowers

Sarah found the gillyflowers blooming beside the old garden wall, their petals glowing crimson, gold, and violet in the morning sun. Her grandmother had planted them many years before, saying they symbolized lasting affection.

Every spring, Sarah carefully tended the flowers. Their sweet, spicy fragrance reminded her of warm afternoons spent listening to her grandmother’s stories. Though the garden had changed over time, the gillyflowers returned faithfully each year.

To Sarah, they were more than flowers. They were a living memory—a quiet promise that love, when cared for, could bloom again and again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem dedicated “for Sarah when she’s older,” featuring a sad-eyed man in a painting, flowers, an apple, a Japanese box, and blurred boundaries between the observer and the observed.
counterfactuals.output:
**for Sarah when she’s older**

In the painting, a sad-eyed man stands beside a table where the flowers have forgotten whether they are blooming or burning. Their petals drift upward like small red boats. An apple waits among them, green on one side, night on the other.

I watch him watching it.

Behind his shoulder rests a Japanese box, black lacquered, with a gold bird flying across the lid. Each evening the bird moves one feather farther. Each evening the man’s eyes become more like mine.

When I open the box, I find the room inside: the table, the flowers, the divided apple, the painting on the wall. A woman stands before it with her hand raised. She is older than I am. She is you, perhaps, reading this. Or she is the man, dreaming himself observed.

The flowers lean out of the canvas to breathe. The apple rolls across the frame and stops in my palm. Its skin is warm.

“Who is real?” I ask.

The sad-eyed man closes my eyes.

Then everything becomes gold lacquer and distance: the room folded into the box, the box folded into the apple, the apple held gently by the painted hand. Outside, someone is watching us grow older.

Sarah, when you find the bird has flown from the lid, do not be afraid. Look closely at the empty place it leaves.

That is where the world enters you.

That is where you enter the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a whimsical, melancholic short piece in the style of an illustrated children’s story for adults. Include a round man who puffs cigars “as if he were alive” and a conversation about memory, failing eyesight, and inaccessible beauty.
counterfactuals.output:
### The Museum of Faraway Things

At the edge of town stood a museum with no doors.

Its curator was a round man named Mr. Thimble, who sat beneath a green umbrella and puffed cigars **as if he were alive**. Each evening, he polished the brass sign:

**THE MUSEUM OF FARAWAY THINGS**  
*Admission: One Memory*

A girl called Elsie came often, though she had never been inside.

“What do you keep in there?” she asked.

“Blue mountains,” said Mr. Thimble. “A silver orchard. A staircase that climbs into the sea.”

“Have you seen them?”

“Once.”

“And now?”

Mr. Thimble removed his spectacles and breathed upon them. His eyes were pale and cloudy, like two moons behind winter glass.

“My eyesight is failing,” he said. “Everything beautiful is moving farther away.”

Elsie sat beside him. “Then remember it.”

“Memory,” he replied, “is a lantern with a moth inside. It gives light, but it also eats the flame.”

They listened to the museum being quiet.

“Could I remember for you?” Elsie asked.

Mr. Thimble smiled. “You might. But then it would become your beauty, not mine.”

Above them, a small painted window showed a golden bird flying over a violet hill. It was too high to reach and too dim for Mr. Thimble to see.

“Is that one of the faraway things?” Elsie asked.

“No,” he said. “That is only the picture of one.”

The moon rose. Mr. Thimble’s cigar went out, though the smoke continued upward for a little while, uncertain of what had happened.

Elsie took his hand.

Together they sat before the doorless museum, guarding all the lovely things neither of them could enter.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dreamlike ekphrastic prose poem about looking at a still-life painting containing gillyflowers, purple bells, an apple, and a grassy hill. Explore reading, sight, memory, identity, and the uncertain difference between art and life.
counterfactuals.output:
**Still Life with Borrowed Weather**

At first I read the painting as if it were a letter left open in a language I had forgotten. The gillyflowers crowded the vase with their small, scented flames; the purple bells leaned outward, listening for a sound beyond the frame. An apple rested on the table, red enough to be a word, round enough to contain the mouth that might speak it. Behind them, impossibly near, a grassy hill rose into a pale weather, green as the first page of childhood.

Looking became a kind of remembering. I knew the hill, though I had never climbed it. I knew the apple’s cool weight, though my hands remained folded in the museum light. Somewhere, a former self ran through the grass carrying a book with blank pages, and wherever the pages turned, flowers appeared. Or perhaps the flowers were already there, reading me—each petal an eye, each bell a little violet ear.

The longer I looked, the less certain I became of which side held the stillness. The painted apple seemed to breathe beneath its skin. The real room dimmed and flattened; visitors passed like brushstrokes. My reflection hovered in the varnish, faintly superimposed upon the vase, so that my face filled with stems and my eyes became two dark seeds. I thought: this is identity, to be arranged by another hand among objects one did not choose, and yet to glow briefly as if chosen.

A memory opened—not mine, perhaps, but the painter’s, or the apple’s: a kitchen after rain, someone reading by a window, the slow tolling of purple flowers in a garden. I could not tell whether I had lived it or merely seen it painted. Is sight only memory arriving early? Is reading the name we give to entering what cannot open?

When I turned away, the hill remained behind my eyes. The gillyflowers followed with their quiet fire. In my pocket I felt the impossible heaviness of an apple, though I had brought nothing with me. Outside, the world appeared meticulously composed: clouds placed in blue, trees stippled with light, every passerby carrying a hidden vase of selves.

I walked on carefully, afraid to touch anything.

The bells were still ringing, though no wind moved them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a lyrical bedtime story addressed to a girl named Sarah for when she is older. Make it strange and bittersweet, with repeated phrases, impossible images, and a sad-eyed painted man who eventually writes the narrator into his landscape.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Country Behind the Blue Door**

Sarah, when you are older, you may remember a door that never belonged to any house.

It was blue in the morning, green at noon, and at night it became the color of a word no one had spoken yet. It stood alone at the edge of a field, with a brass handle warm as a sleeping bird.

Behind it lived a painted man with sad eyes.

Or perhaps he did not live there. Perhaps he was only waiting.

This was long ago, Sarah. This will happen tomorrow.

The painted man wore a coat the color of rain. His hands were narrow and white, and from each fingertip hung a tiny silver bell. Yet when he moved, the bells made no sound.

“Why are your eyes so sad?” I asked him.

“Because I have seen the end of everything,” he said.

“And what happens at the end?”

He looked past me, into the impossible country of his painting.

“Everything begins again,” he said.

Everything begins again.  
Everything begins again.  
But never in quite the same way.

His landscape stretched from the blue door to the farthest fold of sleep. There were upside-down mountains with roots tangled in the stars. There were black swans swimming through the sky, leaving ripples among the clouds. A river climbed a hill and poured itself carefully into the moon.

Along its banks grew clocks with golden leaves.

Each clock kept a different hour.

One said: **Now.**  
One said: **Almost.**  
One said: **Too late.**

The painted man carried a brush made from the whiskers of winter. Every evening he dipped it into a jar of darkness and painted one more thing into his country: a fox with a cathedral in its chest, a ladder descending into the sun, a little red boat sailing through a wheat field.

“Why do you keep painting?” I asked.

“Because the country is lonely.”

“Are you lonely?”

“I am painted,” he answered, as though that explained everything.

Perhaps it did.

Night after night, I returned through the blue door. Night after night, the sad-eyed man stood beside his river that ran uphill. Sometimes we spoke. Sometimes we listened to the silent bells on his fingers.

He painted a forest where the trees dreamed of becoming ships.

He painted a town inhabited only by shadows whose people had gone away.

He painted a great white deer carrying dawn between its antlers.

And once, Sarah, he painted you.

Not as you are now, tucked beneath your blankets with the dark gathered softly around you. He painted you older, walking alone along the riverbank. Your hair was threaded with rain. In one hand you held a key; in the other, a small and stubborn flame.

“Where is she going?” I whispered.

“Home,” said the painted man.

“But she is walking away from the door.”

“Yes,” he said. “That is sometimes how one goes home.”

That is sometimes how one goes home.  
That is sometimes how one goes home.

Years passed outside the painting. Or minutes. Time behaves strangely near a blue door.

My face changed. My voice changed. People I loved became photographs, and photographs became boxes, and boxes became dust beneath beds in houses where nobody remembered my name.

But the painted man remained as he had always been: rain-colored coat, silver bells, sad eyes.

Only his landscape grew brighter.

At last there came a night when the moon was missing. In its place hung an enormous sleeping fish, pale and luminous, breathing tides over the roofs of the world.

The painted man held out his brush.

“I have almost finished,” he said.

I looked into his country. The black swans slept in the clouds. The clock-trees had shed their hours. The white deer knelt at the edge of dawn.

“And then?” I asked.

“Then the door will close.”

“Will I still be able to visit?”

“No.”

The word fell between us like a little stone into a bottomless well.

I wanted to tell him that this was unfair. I wanted to ask who would listen to his silent bells, who would watch the river pour itself into the moon, who would remember the fox with the cathedral in its chest.

Instead I said, “Will you be lonely?”

The painted man smiled. It was the saddest smile I had ever seen.

“Not if you stay.”

Then he dipped his brush into the dark.

Before I could step back, he wrote my name across the sky. He wrote my hands into the branches of the dreaming forest. He wrote my breath into the mist above the river. He wrote my footsteps along the road where your older self walked with her key and her flame.

Last of all, he wrote my heart into the little red boat sailing through the wheat.

I became smaller and farther away.

The blue door narrowed to a line.

Beyond it, I could see my old room, my empty chair, my cup still waiting on the table. Morning entered through the window and touched everything I would never touch again.

I wanted to grieve.

But the painted man took my hand, and though his fingers were made of paint, they were warm.

“Listen,” he said.

For the first time, the silver bells rang.

They sounded like snow falling upward. They sounded like forgotten names being spoken kindly. They sounded like goodbye, Sarah, but also like sleep.

Goodbye, but also sleep.  
Goodbye, but also sleep.

So if, when you are older, you find a blue door standing where no house has ever been, you may open it.

You may see a river climbing toward the moon. You may see an old red boat among the wheat. You may see a sad-eyed man painting beneath the upside-down mountains.

And somewhere in the landscape, someone will be waving to you.

Do not be afraid if you cannot remember who.

Raise your little flame. Turn your key in the evening air.

Then walk on, Sarah.

Walk on toward home.

Even if home lies ahead of you.  
Even if home lies behind.

Everything begins again.

Everything begins again.

But never in quite the same way.
